strengths: Proposes a well-motivated method (LongMab-PO) that models context chunk selection during preference-pair sampling as a UCB-based multi-armed bandit problem, an intuitively appealing improvement over static similarity-based chunk sampling used in prior work (e.g., LOGO/Tang et al.).

The paper includes fairly extensive ablations isolating the contribution of the bandit mechanism (Random-Dist, Final-Dist, Initial-Dist, Direct-PO), which convincingly show that the iterative rollout collection (not just the final learned distribution) is important.

Additional analyses on diversity of sampled responses (embedding similarity mean/variance), evolution of ground-truth chunk recall and SubEM over rollout steps, the effect of the number of selected chunks K, and reward formulation (full-response vs answer-based SubEM) add useful mechanistic insight beyond headline numbers.
A qualitative case study illustrates the intended benefit (mitigating lost-in-the-middle) in a concrete multi-hop example.
The probe-based UCB initialization is a reasonable and well-motivated solution to the bandit cold-start problem, grounded in citation/evidence-extraction ideas from prior work.
weaknesses: The reward signal used to guide the MAB rollout (SubEM/F1 against ground truth) is the same family of metric used for downstream evaluation, raising concern about the reported gains partly reflecting reward-metric alignment rather than genuine long-context reasoning improvement; no held-out or human-judged quality metric is used to corroborate results.

Improvements are inconsistent across backbones: for Qwen-2.5-7B, per-dataset performance is frequently below LongFaith-PO or other DPO baselines (e.g., MuSiQue, 2WikiMQA SubEM), and only the aggregate average favors LongMab-PO, weakening the claim of "consistently outperforming baselines."

Test sets are quite small (150–351 examples per dataset), and no variance/standard deviation across multiple runs or significance testing is reported, making it hard to assess whether the reported gains (often a few points) are robust or within noise.

Training relies solely on MuSiQue-derived synthetic long-context data (extended with random Wikipedia passages to 8–16k tokens); generalization claims to longer, more realistic contexts (e.g., 190k-token FakebookQA) rest on a narrow and somewhat artificial training distribution.

No discussion of the computational overhead of 30-round MAB rollouts (extra LLM calls per training example) relative to baseline sampling strategies, which is an important practical consideration for reproducibility and fair comparison.

Chunking is uniform/fixed-length (1,500 tokens) rather than semantically informed, and the method's sensitivity to chunk size itself is not explored, leaving open whether gains are robust to this design choice.

The novelty is primarily a recombination of existing components (UCB bandit exploration, DPO, LLM-based evidence probing) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism, and the related work on RL/bandit exploration for LLM sampling is not deeply engaged beyond citation.

strengths: The core idea of modeling long-context chunks as arms of a multi-armed bandit and using UCB to adaptively guide chunk selection for response sampling is a well-motivated and reasonably novel extension of prior static/similarity-based chunk sampling (e.g., Tang et al. 2024), directly targeting the noted limitation of non-adaptive exploration.

The paper includes a thorough set of ablations isolating the contribution of each design choice: comparison against Random-Dist, Final-Dist, and Initial-Dist chunk selection strategies convincingly shows that the iterative bandit rollout (not just chunk-aware sampling in general) is responsible for most of the gains.

Additional analyses (recall of ground-truth chunks over rollout steps, diversity via embedding similarity variance, reward-design ablation between full-response vs. answer-based SubEM, and sensitivity to K) provide a fairly complete picture of why and how the method works, going beyond simple leaderboard-style reporting.

Experiments span two different backbone LLMs (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct) and five datasets from two benchmarks (LongBench, InfiniteBench), including out-of-domain generalization from training only on MuSiQue, which strengthens the practical relevance claim.
A concrete case study illustrates qualitatively how the method mitigates lost-in-the-middle failures relative to a strong baseline (LongFaith-PO), aiding interpretability of the quantitative gains.

The paper is clearly written, with a well-illustrated framework (Figures 1–2) and sufficiently detailed implementation description (hyperparameters, training setup, prompts in the appendix) to support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Results on Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct are mixed: LongMab-PO does not achieve the best SubEM on several individual datasets (e.g., MuSiQue, 2WikiMQA, MFQA-En) and is only clearly best in aggregate/F1, which somewhat undercuts the 'state-of-the-art' framing and suggests the method's advantage may be backbone-dependent or metric-dependent.

Evaluation sets are small (150–351 examples per dataset, MuSiQue/2WikiMQA/NarrativeQA at 200), and no variance/significance information (multiple seeds, confidence intervals) is reported, making it hard to assess whether the reported gains over closely competing baselines (e.g., LongFaith-PO on Llama) are statistically robust.

The computational cost of the method (30 rollout rounds requiring 30 LLM generations plus a probing LLM call per training example) is not analyzed or compared against the generation budget used by baselines (LongReward-PO, SeaLong-PO, LongFaith-PO); it is unclear whether comparisons are budget-matched in terms of number of LLM calls, which affects the fairness of the comparison and practical cost-benefit assessment.

The evaluation relies solely on SubEM and F1, both fairly shallow lexical-overlap metrics for QA; no human evaluation or LLM-judge-based quality assessment is included to corroborate claims about 'higher-quality' responses, despite quality being a central claim of the paper.

Sensitivity to the fixed chunk size (1,500 tokens) and the fixed number of chunks n is not explored beyond varying K (number of selected chunks); cases where the answer span crosses chunk boundaries are not discussed, which is a plausible failure mode of any chunk-based method.

The probe-based initialization uses the ground-truth answer to generate a reasoning trace for computing initial expected rewards; while this is only used to build training data (not at test time) and thus not a leakage problem per se, the paper could more clearly justify/ablate how sensitive downstream performance is to the quality of this probe step versus other initialization schemes (e.g., uniform).

strengths: Introduces a reasonably novel formulation of chunk selection for preference-pair construction in long-context DPO as a Multi-Armed Bandit problem, integrating UCB-based exploration/exploitation with a probe-based initialization to mitigate cold-start, which is a sensible extension over prior heuristic/relevance-only chunk-sampling approaches (e.g., Logo-PO).

Extensive ablation studies isolate the contribution of individual components (UCB scoring, probe initialization, number of chunks K, rollout steps T, exploration factor alpha, reward formulation), which supports the internal validity of the claimed mechanism.

Additional generalization experiments across model families/sizes (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B/14B, Qwen3-8B) and to substantially longer test-time contexts (LV-Eval up to 128k) strengthen confidence that gains are not an artifact of a single backbone or evaluation length.

Mechanistic analyses (ground-truth recall over rollouts, LLM-judged chunk-set quality, chunk selection frequency distribution, response diversity/variance) provide converging evidence for why the method works, going beyond simple leaderboard comparisons.
Reasonably comprehensive baseline suite covering SFT and multiple recent DPO-based long-context methods, plus a qualitative case study illustrating alleviation of the lost-in-the-middle phenomenon.
weaknesses: The reward used to drive MAB rollouts (average of SubEM and F1) is the same family of metric used for final evaluation, creating a risk that gains partly reflect optimizing toward the evaluation metric rather than genuine improvements in long-context comprehension; this potential circularity is not discussed or controlled for.

Reported improvements are inconsistent across backbones: for Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, LongMab's average SubEM (37.06) is only marginally better than SeaLong-PO (36.71) and worse than LongFaith-PO on individual datasets (e.g., MuSiQue: 48.50 vs 44.00; MFQA-En: LongMab underperforms even the vanilla LLM), somewhat undercutting the abstract's claim of a general 'more than 4%' improvement, which mainly holds for the Llama backbone and F1 metric.

Training data is derived from a single source dataset (MuSiQue augmented with Wikipedia distractors) at a fixed context-length regime (8k-16k); while some longer-context and cross-model generalization tests are included, the core training pipeline's dependence on one QA dataset limits certainty about broader applicability to other task types (e.g., summarization) mentioned as motivation in the intro.

No variance/significance reporting (single run per setting appears to be used, given fixed seed 42), leaving open whether observed differences, especially the small margins on Qwen, are robust rather than noise.

The method incurs substantially higher training-data-construction cost (up to 30 rollout LLM calls plus a probe/reasoning-trace generation and embedding computation per example) relative to baselines, but this computational overhead is not quantified or compared against baselines in terms of cost-effectiveness, despite being acknowledged qualitatively in the limitations.

The probe-based initialization requires access to the ground-truth answer to generate a reasoning trace for reward initialization; while apparently used only at training-data-construction time, this dependency and its implications (e.g., applicability only in domains with labeled QA pairs) could be stated more explicitly and analyzed for sensitivity to probe quality/reasoning-trace errors.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated problem (lost-in-the-middle, noisy preference data for long-context DPO) with a reasonably novel technical mechanism: framing chunk selection as a UCB-guided multi-armed bandit rollout, combined with a probe-based initialization to alleviate cold-start.

Extensive empirical validation: main results on two backbones (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B) across 5 datasets/benchmarks, plus appendix experiments on additional model scales/types (Qwen2.5-14B, Qwen3-8B) and out-of-distribution longer contexts (16k-128k, LV-Eval), showing the method is not overfit to a single setting.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of UCB updating vs. probe initialization vs. random/direct sampling, as well as sensitivity analyses for K, rollout steps T, exploration factor α, and reward-design choices, which substantiate the claimed mechanism rather than just reporting end-task numbers.

Mechanistic analyses (ground-truth recall over rollouts, LLM-judged chunk-set quality along four dimensions, chunk selection frequency distribution, response diversity/variance) provide converging evidence for *why* the method improves preference-pair quality, going beyond a black-box performance comparison.

Clear presentation with illustrative figures, prompts, and a qualitative case study that concretely shows the intended benefit (integrating dispersed multi-hop evidence) versus a representative baseline.
weaknesses: The MAB reward (Eq. 4) and the probe-based initialization (Eq. 8) both directly use the ground-truth answer y*, so the 'exploration under uncertainty' framing is somewhat overstated: this is closer to an oracle-guided combinatorial search for constructing offline training data than a bandit problem with genuinely unknown rewards; this should be more explicitly acknowledged, and its implications for cost/generality (every rollout scoring step needs gold answers) discussed.

Computational cost is non-trivial (T=30 rollout LLM calls per training instance) and is only briefly acknowledged as a limitation without quantification (e.g., wall-clock/GPU-hours vs. baselines), making it hard to judge the practical trade-off against simpler heuristic chunk-sampling baselines like Logo-PO.

Gains are not uniform across all datasets/metrics: e.g., on Qwen-2.5-7B, LongFaith-PO surpasses LongMab on MuSiQue SubEM (48.50 vs 44.00), and several individual-dataset comparisons in Table 1 are mixed rather than a clean sweep, which tempers the strength of the 'consistently outperforms all baselines' claim.

No variance/multiple-run statistics or significance testing are reported for the main results, which is a concern given the known noisiness of SubEM/F1 metrics and the relatively small evaluation sets (e.g., 150-200 examples for several LongBench subsets).

Training data is derived exclusively from one multi-hop QA dataset (MuSiQue) with fixed equal-length token chunking; while OOD QA generalization is tested, the paper's broader motivating claims about summarization and other long-context task types (raised in the intro) are never empirically evaluated.

It is unclear whether baseline numbers (LongFaith-PO, Logo-PO, LongReward-PO, SeaLong-PO) are reproduced in-house under matched conditions or taken from original papers/checkpoints; if reproduced, reproduction fidelity/hyperparameter matching is not discussed, raising a fairness concern for the comparisons.
Code/data release is only promised ('will be released'), so full reproducibility cannot yet be independently verified, despite detailed hyperparameters and prompts being provided in the appendix.
